title: Strings, Booleans, and None Assessment
description: Multiple-choice assessment for Strings, Booleans, and None.

questions.question: What practical problem does this lesson help solve?

options.text: Programs need more than numbers: names, flags, and missing values are everywhere.
It lets you avoid running code completely.
It replaces the need for readable variable names.
It is mainly theoretical and has little effect on implementation quality.

questions.explanation: Programs need more than numbers: names, flags, and missing values are everywhere.

questions.question: Which practice best supports the lesson workflow?

options.text: Write a large program before testing smaller parts.
Predict the output, run a small example, then change one value.
Ignore output as long as the editor has no red underline.
Copy code without understanding the data it uses.

questions.explanation: Small prediction loops build real debugging skill.

questions.question: What is the safest beginner habit when this concept feels confusing?

options.text: Add more code until the error disappears.
Delete the line that creates the error without reading it.
Print the important value, inspect its type, and test a smaller case.
Use shorter variable names so the code looks advanced.

questions.explanation: Reducing the problem and inspecting data makes debugging faster.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the core idea?

options.text: The main goal is to memorize every symbol before running anything.
The concept is only useful after learning advanced frameworks.
The best program is the one with the most lines.
A string stores text, a boolean stores True or False, and None represents no value yet. These types make program state readable.

questions.explanation: A string stores text, a boolean stores True or False, and None represents no value yet. These types make program state readable.
